In short

  • The clearest finding: Higher any_ht goes together with higher died. 4 of the methods used agreed on this.
  • 10 variable(s) in total showed a relationship with died.
  • Everything here was measured at a single point in time. That means we can say these variables move together, but not which one comes first, and not that one causes the other.

What this report can and cannot tell you

Finding that two things go together is not the same as showing that one causes the other. Two variables can move together because a third thing drives both of them. Ice cream sales and sunburn rise together, but ice cream does not cause sunburn: hot weather causes both.

Agreement between methods does not fix this. If every method is looking at the same data, and something that was never measured is driving both variables, then every method will report the same relationship and every one of them will be misled in the same way. High agreement means the finding is stable, not that it is causal.

How to read this report

Each relationship gets a score from 0 to 100 called the evidence score. It is built from three separate things, and it helps to keep them apart:

Size

How big the relationship is. A large value means that when one variable changes, the other changes a lot.

Precision

How sure we are of the number itself. This grows with the number of samples and shrinks when the estimate is noisy.

Agreement

How many of the analysis methods saw the same thing. Several methods were run on the same data; this counts how many agreed.

What this report can and cannot tell you

Finding that two things go together is not the same as showing that one causes the other. Two variables can move together because a third thing drives both of them. Ice cream sales and sunburn rise together, but ice cream does not cause sunburn: hot weather causes both.

Agreement between methods does not fix this. If every method is looking at the same data, and something that was never measured is driving both variables, then every method will report the same relationship and every one of them will be misled in the same way. High agreement means the finding is stable, not that it is causal.

Because of that, every relationship below is labelled with how much can be claimed about cause:

Observed together

The two were seen to move together and nothing else was taken into account. This is the weakest claim.

Other factors accounted for

Known factors were subtracted out. This is stronger, but only for the factors that were actually measured. Anything not measured is still unaccounted for.

Measured in order

The first variable was measured before the second. That rules out the relationship running backwards, which is real progress, but it still does not rule out a third factor driving both.

Instrumented

A special kind of variable was used that, under strong assumptions, does support a causal reading.

Does one number describe everybody?

Every figure in this report is an average over the people who were measured, and an average says nothing about whether they resemble each other. The same number can mean the relationship holds in everyone, or that it is strong in a tenth of them and absent in the rest. Those are different findings: the first is about the group, the second is about ten people nobody has identified.

So each of the 14 strongest relationships was asked how much of the group would have to be removed to halve it. For a relationship that holds broadly the answer is most of them, because removing a few people barely shifts an average. 14 here were halved by removing 5% or less.

Nothing was named as a possible modifier, so no subgroup was tested directly. Passing heterogeneity = a metadata column asks whether each relationship differs across it.

Measured values and filled-in values

Some of the variables here arrived with gaps. Rather than throw those people away, preprocessing estimated what the missing numbers probably were. That is standard practice and usually the right call, but it has a consequence nothing downstream can see: once a gap is filled, no model can tell a measurement from an estimate, and the confidence intervals come out exactly as narrow as if every value had been real.

163 of the relationships in this report involve a variable that was partly filled in. Their scores were scaled down in proportion to how much was filled and how much the filling method preserves — the most affected keeps 81% of what its statistics alone would earn. Nothing else about them was changed.

Each was also refitted using only the people whose value was actually measured. 2 of 20 changed direction. A relationship that reverses when the estimated values are removed was produced by the filling, not found in the data.

Sample size is a separate matter and is already in the precision score. This is only about values that were reconstructed.

No causal diagram was supplied

Every label above was inferred from the shape of the study alone: what was measured, when, and what was adjusted for. That tells you a model controlled for something; it cannot tell you whether the right something was controlled for.

If you are willing to commit to a diagram of what causes what, pass it as analyze(..., dag = ) and each relationship will be checked against it. Adjusting for a variable that sits between the exposure and the outcome, or for one the outcome itself causes, makes an estimate worse rather than better, and nothing in the data will reveal that.

What these methods are

logistic regression

Fits a straight line between the variable and the outcome, after subtracting the effect of any factors you asked it to account for.

What it cannot tell you. It cannot tell which one came first, and it can only account for factors that were actually measured.

elastic net

Fits every variable at once and shrinks the useless ones to exactly zero, so what survives is a short list that predicts the outcome together.

What it cannot tell you. When two variables carry the same information it keeps one and drops the other, so being dropped is not evidence of having no effect.

random forest importance

Builds hundreds of decision trees and measures how much worse the predictions get when one variable is scrambled. A big drop means the variable carried real information.

What it cannot tell you. It measures usefulness for prediction, not the size or the direction of an effect. Something downstream of the outcome predicts it beautifully.

Bayesian network (hill climbing)

Searches for a network of arrows that explains the observed pattern of correlations with as few connections as possible.

What it cannot tell you. Several different arrangements of arrows explain the same data equally well, so the direction it picks is often one of many that fit.

What would settle this

Each of these follows from a specific weakness in this relationship rather than from general caution, so they are in the order the evidence puts them.

  1. Measure a confounder of any_ht and died. To erase this it would have to be associated with both at a risk ratio of at least 3.6; anything weaker leaves the relationship standing.
  2. Measure any_ht before died in the same people. Nothing in this data establishes which came first, and the reverse direction fits it equally well.
  3. Replicate in a cohort collected independently. Here the estimate is halved by removing 15 people, so it may describe them rather than the population.
  4. Measure ever_osteo_arthritis in the people whose value was filled in. Part of this estimate rests on numbers that were reconstructed rather than observed.

What these methods are

logistic regression

Fits a straight line between the variable and the outcome, after subtracting the effect of any factors you asked it to account for.

What it cannot tell you. It cannot tell which one came first, and it can only account for factors that were actually measured.

elastic net

Fits every variable at once and shrinks the useless ones to exactly zero, so what survives is a short list that predicts the outcome together.

What it cannot tell you. When two variables carry the same information it keeps one and drops the other, so being dropped is not evidence of having no effect.

random forest importance

Searches for a network of arrows that explains the observed pattern of correlations with as few connections as possible.

structural equation model

Fits all the candidate variables against the outcome simultaneously, so each estimate is adjusted for the others.

What it cannot tell you. The structure it fits was written automatically, not derived from biology. It is a multivariable regression, despite the name.

What would settle this

Each of these follows from a specific weakness in this relationship rather than from general caution, so they are in the order the evidence puts them.

  1. Measure and adjust for the common causes of LBXHCY and died.
  2. Measure LBXHCY before died in the same people. Nothing in this data establishes which came first, and the reverse direction fits it equally well.
  3. Replicate in a cohort collected independently. Here the estimate is halved by removing 10 people, so it may describe them rather than the population.
  4. Measure ever_osteo_arthritis in the people whose value was filled in. Part of this estimate rests on numbers that were reconstructed rather than observed.
  5. Treat this as an artefact until the missing values are measured: on the observed rows alone the relationship points the other way.
  6. Separate LBXHCY from the 2 other variables it moves with. In this data they cannot be told apart, so the effect may belong to any of them or to whatever drives all of them.

What these methods are

logistic regression

Fits a straight line between the variable and the outcome, after subtracting the effect of any factors you asked it to account for.

What it cannot tell you. It cannot tell which one came first, and it can only account for factors that were actually measured.

random forest importance

Builds hundreds of decision trees and measures how much worse the predictions get when one variable is scrambled. A big drop means the variable carried real information.

What it cannot tell you. It measures usefulness for prediction, not the size or the direction of an effect. Something downstream of the outcome predicts it beautifully.

What would settle this

Each of these follows from a specific weakness in this relationship rather than from general caution, so they are in the order the evidence puts them.

  1. Measure a confounder of DR1TVB1 and died. To erase this it would have to be associated with both at a risk ratio of at least 2.5; anything weaker leaves the relationship standing.
  2. Measure DR1TVB1 before died in the same people. Nothing in this data establishes which came first, and the reverse direction fits it equally well.
  3. Replicate in a cohort collected independently. Here the estimate is halved by removing 16 people, so it may describe them rather than the population.
  4. Measure ever_osteo_arthritis in the people whose value was filled in. Part of this estimate rests on numbers that were reconstructed rather than observed.
  5. Separate DR1TVB1 from the 28 other variables it moves with. In this data they cannot be told apart, so the effect may belong to any of them or to whatever drives all of them.

Things measured many times

Measured variables are often not separate things. Variables that rise and fall together are usually one underlying process measured several times over. Grouping them and testing the group asks the question directly, instead of asking it once per variable and reporting the answer as many findings.

These are not extra evidence

A group and the variables inside it are the same measurements at two resolutions. If a group and its members both appear in this report they agree because they are made of each other, and neither one confirms the other. Count the finding once.

Groups were formed by clustering variables on how strongly they move together, at a correlation of 0.50 or more. Variables that move independently were left alone.

What this does and does not tell you

A resample draws from the people who were actually measured, so this says how much the picture depends on which of them ended up in the study. It is not evidence that any relationship is real.

A variable with no connection to the outcome that happens to track it in this sample will track it in almost every resample of that sample too, and will look perfectly stable here. The question of whether these relationships exceed what the same analysis finds on noise is a different one, answered by null calibration at effort = "thorough".

All relationships together form a map. Variables that connect to many others are shown as hubs; variables that sit between two different kinds of measurement are shown as bridges.

The methods behind these results

Each looks at the data differently, which is the point: agreement between methods that share no assumptions says more than one method repeated. Each carries a level describing what kind of claim it can support, and agreement is weighted by that level rather than counted.

Bayesian network structurelevel 2, associational

Searches for a network of arrows that explains the observed pattern of correlations with as few connections as possible.

What it cannot tell you. Several different arrangements of arrows explain the same data equally well, so the direction it picks is often one of many that fit.

Adjusted associationlevel 2, associational

Fits a straight line between the variable and the outcome, after subtracting the effect of any factors you asked it to account for.

What it cannot tell you. It cannot tell which one came first, and it can only account for factors that were actually measured.

Elastic net selectionlevel 1, predictive

Fits every variable at once and shrinks the useless ones to exactly zero, so what survives is a short list that predicts the outcome together.

What it cannot tell you. When two variables carry the same information it keeps one and drops the other, so being dropped is not evidence of having no effect.

Random forest importancelevel 1, predictive

Builds hundreds of decision trees and measures how much worse the predictions get when one variable is scrambled. A big drop means the variable carried real information.

What it cannot tell you. It measures usefulness for prediction, not the size or the direction of an effect. Something downstream of the outcome predicts it beautifully.

Structural equation modellevel 2, associational

Fits all the candidate variables against the outcome simultaneously, so each estimate is adjusted for the others.

What it cannot tell you. The structure it fits was written automatically, not derived from biology. It is a multivariable regression, despite the name.

Every quantity, explained

Evidence score0 to 100

Size, Precision and Agreement multiplied together, then scaled. All three must be reasonable for the score to be high: a large effect measured badly scores low, and so does a tiny effect measured perfectly.

Careful. It is a summary of how well supported a relationship is, not of how important it is biologically.

Size0 to 1

How large the relationship is, put on a common scale so that methods measuring different things can be averaged.

Careful. A big number here means the variables move together a lot, not that one causes the other.

Precision0 to 1

How tightly the number was pinned down. Built from the number of samples, the width of the confidence interval, and the significance after correcting for how many things were tested.

Careful. High precision on a biased estimate just means confidently wrong.

Agreement0 to 1

How many of the methods that looked at this relationship saw it in the same direction, weighted so that stronger kinds of evidence count for more than weaker ones.

Careful. Methods sharing the same blind spot agree with each other. This measures stability, not truth.

Estimateany number

The size of the relationship in the units that particular method works in. A Cox model reports it on a log scale, a random forest reports a drop in prediction quality: they are not comparable across rows.

Careful. Compare estimates within a method, never between methods.

95% CIa range

The range of values compatible with the data. Narrow means well determined.

Careful. If the range crosses zero, the data does not exclude there being no relationship at all.

p-value0 to 1

How surprising this result would be if there were really no relationship. Small means surprising.

Careful. It says nothing about how big or how important the relationship is.

FDR0 to 1

The p-value corrected for having tested many things at once. Test a thousand variables and fifty will look significant by luck; this accounts for that.

Careful. Always read the FDR rather than the raw p-value here.

E-value1 upwards

How strong a hidden factor would have to be, on both the variable and the outcome, to explain the whole relationship away. Near 1 means a trivial one would do it.

Careful. It does not say a hidden factor exists. It says how much would be needed.

Recovered ina percentage

The analysis was repeated on many random re-samples of the same people. This is how often the relationship survived.

Careful. A relationship that disappears in half the resamples is fragile even if its score is high.

Direction confidence0.5 to 1

When methods disagree about which way the arrow points, how one-sided that disagreement was. 0.5 means it was a coin flip.

Careful. Only measurement order settles direction. Everything else is inference.

na count

How many samples that particular method actually used, after dropping any with missing values.

Careful. Different rows can rest on different numbers of people.

Where to find the raw numbers

Nothing here is hidden. In R, on the object this report was built from:

result$evidence[[1]]$contributions   # what every method said
result$effects                       # the same, for every relationship
result$tables$evidence               # the merged and scored relationships
result$diagnostics                   # model fit, resampling, calibration
explain(result, "NAME")              # everything known about one variable

What the analysis is based on

Samples analysed
687
Samples set aside
1113
not measured in every block
Variables examined
150
of 161 available

Only samples present in every block can be compared across blocks, so 1113 were set aside.

Not everything was examined

There were too many variables to test every possible pair, so 150 were carried forward on the strength of their relationship with the outcome. The remaining 11 were not examined for indirect roles and could still matter.

Limitations

Every analysis rests on things that could be otherwise. These apply to the results above and should be read alongside them, not after them.

  • Observational data: no relationship reported here is identified by design.
  • 0 of 181 relationships carry temporal precedence.
  • Agreement between methods measures stability, not validity: methods sharing an unmeasured confounder agree while all being biased.
  • Analysis rests on 687 sample(s) shared by every analysed block; 1113 were dropped by the intersection.
  • The graph was not calibrated against a null. Without that there is no way to know how many of these relationships the engine would find on data with no signal at all; run with permutations > 0.
  • Under 50 bootstrap resamples, 86 of 181 relationships were recovered less than half the time.
  • 11 of 161 features were screened out against the outcome before the pairwise stage and were never examined for indirect roles.

Glossary

Outcome
The thing the analysis is trying to explain.
Variable
Anything that was measured.
Relationship
Two variables that change together in a way unlikely to be chance alone.
Evidence score
A 0-100 summary combining size, precision and agreement.
Adjusted
Other known factors were subtracted out before measuring the relationship.
Confounder
Something not measured that drives two variables at once, making them look related.
Mediator
A variable that sits between a cause and its outcome.
Hub
A variable connected to many others.
